title: The article glued to the end
goal: Master the only way Icelandic says "the": not with a separate word, but with an ending glued to the back of the noun — *bók* "book", *bókin* "the book".
bekal: tell "a book" from "the book" without a single extra word
use *eiga* to say what you own

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Heima hjá Önnu
dialogs.intro: Anna shows Búdí her small apartment in Reykjavík. From the living-room window, Mount Esja is clearly visible.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Þakka þér fyrir. Íbúðin er lítil en góð.
lines.id: Thank you. The apartment is small but nice.
lines.literal: thank you for. apartment-the is small but good.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Eldhúsið er þarna, og stofan er hér.
lines.id: The kitchen is over there, and the living room is here.
lines.literal: kitchen-the is there, and living-room-the is here.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Glugginn er stór! Ég sé fjallið.
lines.id: The window is big! I can see the mountain.
lines.literal: window-the is big! I see mountain-the.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Já, fjallið heitir Esja. Það er fallegt á morgnana.
lines.id: Yes, the mountain is called Esja. It's beautiful in the mornings.
lines.literal: yes, mountain-the is-called Esja. it is beautiful on mornings-the.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Nei, þetta er herbergi systur minnar. Herbergið mitt er þarna.
lines.id: No, this is my sister's room. My room is over there.
lines.literal: no, this is room sister's my. room-the mine is there.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Nei, ég á hjól. Hjólið er úti. Bíllinn er hjá pabba.
lines.id: No, I have a bike. The bike is outside. The car is at Dad's.
lines.literal: no, I own bike. bike-the is outside. car-the is at dad.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Í Jakarta á ég ekki hjól. Þar á ég bíl.
lines.id: In Jakarta I don't have a bike. There I have a car.
lines.literal: in Jakarta own I not bike. there own I car.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Hér er hjólið betra. Bensínið er svo dýrt!
lines.id: Here a bike is better. Gas is so expensive!
lines.literal: here is bike-the better. gasoline-the is so expensive!

notes: **Icelandic has no separate article at all.** There's no word for "the" and no word for "a/an". *Bók* on its own means both "book" and "a book"; for "the book" you add an ending: *bókin*.

**For English speakers, this is the new way of thinking.** Instead of a word in front ("*the* book"), Icelandic adds a tag at the back: *bók* → *bókin*, "book-the". The literal lines in this course write it exactly like that. Swedish, Danish, and Norwegian do the same (*huset*, "house-the"), so you're in good company.
**The ending follows the gender**, so the three genders from Unit 3 come straight into play: *-inn* for kk, *-in* for kvk, *-ið* for hk. That's why Unit 3 comes before this one.

**Í Jakarta á ég ekki hjól — note the word order.** Because the phrase *í Jakarta* takes first place, the verb *á* jumps ahead of the subject. Icelandic locks the verb in **second place**, whatever stands in first place. You already saw the same rule in questions in Unit 1.
**Áttu = átt þú.** The verb *eiga* (to own) has an *ég* form of just one letter: **á**. Don't mix it up with the preposition *á* (on, at) — two completely different words, and both very common.

**Place names often come with the article.** *Fjallið heitir Esja*, and in everyday talk the mountain itself is called *Esjan*. The same habit gives *Bláa lónið* (the Blue Lagoon) and *Hringurinn* (Iceland's Ring Road).

grammars.title: The article: an ending that sticks
body: A table you'll use until the very last unit. The form without the article is what's in the dictionary; the form with it is what you use when speaking.
after: If the basic word already ends in a **vowel**, the ending is shortened so the vowels don't pile up: *stofa* → *stofan* (not *stofain*), *herbergi* → *herbergið* (not *herbergiið*).
The **plural** has its own endings: *hestar* → *hestarnir*, *bækur* → *bækurnar*, *hús* → *húsin*. Plurals come up in Unit 5; for now, just get to know the sound.

grammars.title: Eiga — to own
body: The verb "to have" used for things you own. Its forms are short and irregular, so learn them like a song.
after: ⚠️ **Eiga is not hafa.** *Eiga* is for things you own (*ég á bíl*); *hafa* is for what you have for the moment, or for forming the past (*ég hef tíma* — I have time). When it's about possessions and you're unsure, use *eiga*.
The thing owned appears in the **þolfall** form: *bíll* → *bíl*, *hestur* → *hest*. The endings **-ur** and **-ll** drop off. This case is covered fully in Unit 8; for now, just copy it.

sections.title: The home and what's in it

blocks.text: *Eldhús* literally means "fire-house", and *baðherbergi* "bath-room" — built exactly like the English word. Icelandic compounds can almost always be taken apart like this, and that's the fastest way to grow your vocabulary without a dictionary.
Since there's no separate article, the only difference is whether the ending is there or not. Compare these pairs, and say them out loud:

blocks.title: When to use the article
items: For something **already** mentioned or **clear** to both speakers: *Hvar er bókin?* — the book we both know about.
For something there's only one of nearby: *Glugginn er stór* — the window in this room.
**Not** after *er* for jobs or categories: *Ég er kennari*, not *ég er kennarinn*. Just as English says "I'm a teacher", never "I'm the teacher" in that sense — and Icelandic drops the "a" as well.

exercises.prompt: Add the article to the end of each noun.
Fill in the right form of *eiga*.
Choose the right form: with or without the article.
items: Ég sé ____ (hús, húsið) — það sem við ræddum um í gær.
The room is small but nice.
In Reykjavík I don't have a car.
